_comment: The cast, locations, props and effects a :::dialogue may name. tools/build.py
validates every speaker, emotion, background, prop, effect and balloon shape
against this file and fails on one it does not know — a dialogue that named an
avatar nobody drew would ship as a broken image beside a speech bubble.
Six vocabularies, and the split is deliberate. `characters` and `emotions` are
WHO and WHAT FACE. `backgrounds` is WHERE. `props` are things that exist in the
scene and can be pointed at — a bucket, a board game, a box that will not open.
`fx` are things that do not exist in the scene at all: the manga sign language
of a sweat drop, a shock burst, circling birds. A prop is furniture and can be
picked up; an effect is punctuation and cannot. `bubbles` is HOW a line sounds.
This file declares what EXISTS as a design. The image files themselves arrive
separately; tools/check_cast.py reports which are still missing and does not
fail, so the dialogues can be authored before the art is drawn.
Emotions are deliberately six and shared by every character. A per-character
set would be more expressive and would also mean nobody could ever remember
which ones a given character has. Six x five is thirty avatars, which is a
set one person can actually draw and keep consistent.
An avatar is HALF-BODY, cropped at the waist, not a headshot: two of the five
characters carry their identifying feature on the body rather than the face
(Ba Sau's forearms, Khoa's notebook), and the clothes and build are where
most of the characterisation in this style lives.
ONE FILE PER CHARACTER, not one per emotion. The generated sheet IS the
asset: six panels in a row, saved whole as art/cast/<slug>.webp, which the
build copies to docs/assets/cast/, and the page shows one
panel by offsetting it. That removes the cutting step, which was the most
error-prone part of the pipeline — six files that had to share a width, a
height and a baseline or the character jumped between lines. It also takes
the cast from thirty files to five.
`col` is the panel's position in the sheet and is therefore LOAD-BEARING:
it is the offset the page uses. It must match the left-to-right order the
prompt asks for. Reordering these without regenerating the art silently
gives every character the wrong face. Ti's six drawings already exist against
this order — do not touch it.
research/story/illustration-prompts.md is where these are drawn from, and the
slugs here are the filenames it tells you to save.
One sheet is `cols` x `rows` equal panels in a single image of `aspect`.
A panel is therefore aspect*rows/cols wide for its height — at 3 x 2 in a
3:2 image that is exactly 1.0, a SQUARE panel, which is the point: a square
frame has room for folded arms and a raised hand without clipping them.
A 6 x 1 strip would need a 6:1 image, which is an extreme ratio to ask a
generator for. 3 x 2 at 3:2 is an ordinary photo ratio and gives the same
six panels.
The page derives both the crop and the element's shape from these three
numbers alone, so nothing in the CSS or the markup hard-codes the grid.

neutral.is: Talking, unremarkable. The default, and the one used most.

happy.is: Pleased, warm, amused. A real smile.

worried.is: Anxious or concerned — brows up and together.

annoyed.is: Cross, exasperated, digging in. Brows down.

surprised.is: Caught out, startled. Eyes wide, mouth open.

_characters_comment: Five, and the same five all year. Ti and Thao are drawn and written and do
not change. Bong occupies the slot the cat used to: she is the magic, she is
the one who can call, and she is the reason the sea is coming.
Diacritics matter here for a reason that has nothing to do with art. A key a
learner has to TYPE must never contain one — Khoa is safe, Bong is not.

Thảo.who: his friend, the one who believes him

Bống.who: the sea-child; ashore about a week, and only she can call things back

Bà Sáu.who: his grandmother; sells at the fish market before light

Khoa.who: top of everything, and kind about it

_backgrounds_comment: Eleven plates for a coastal city. Four of them are the fixed furniture the
whole year recycles — harbour-wall, kitchen, school-yard, fish-market — and
the rest are the places a particular chapter needs and then gives back.
The place is Quy Nhon on the central coast, and it is real. Bai Se, the
fishing quarter these plates are set in, is not: it is invented so that no
real street is given a fictional poverty. Ghenh Rang, Thap Doi, Nhon Ly and
the whale shrine at Lang Ong Nam Hai are real and are painted as they are.

backgrounds.harbour-wall: The concrete harbour wall at Bãi Sẻ — the tide line, moored boats, chalk marks climbing the wall, the bay beyond
backgrounds.kitchen: Bà Sáu's kitchen — low table, enamel bowls, dried fish, a doorway of hot white light
backgrounds.school-yard: The school yard — concrete, a painted noticeboard, a flame tree, the sea below the wall
backgrounds.fish-market: The port market before light — baskets, crushed ice, bare bulbs, everyone talking at once
backgrounds.lane: The steep lane down to the water, evening, light from open doorways
backgrounds.town-beach: The city beach and its promenade — palms, hotels, a crescent of sand, the headland at the end
backgrounds.science-room: The school science room after hours — desk lamp, wires, a darkening window
backgrounds.flooded-street: The street under water — boats where the buses were, people on the roofs, quiet
backgrounds.cliff-road: The headland road at first light, the lighthouse at the end of it, open sea below
backgrounds.whale-temple: The whale shrine on the sand at festival night — lanterns, offerings, the bones in the dark of the hall
backgrounds.under-water: Under the harbour — coral through the moorings, shafts of green light, a slow shape further out

_stage_comment: How many people may stand in one panel, and where they stand.
`max_cast` is FOUR and the build fails on a fifth. The limit is not layout, it
is legibility: the avatars are half-body and the panel is one square-ish frame,
so four figures are already about 22% of the frame's width each. A fifth is a
silhouette, and a silhouette cannot carry an expression — which is the entire
reason there are six drawings of every face. A scene that genuinely needs five
people should be two panels, and splitting it is free: put a @cast line between
two spoken lines and the beat breaks there.
Figures are laid out left to right in the order they arrive on stage, spread
across the floor of the panel, and the SPEAKER is the one at full strength —
everyone else is held back a little. That is what replaces the name label that
used to sit on every balloon: with more than two people on stage, who is
talking has to be shown in the picture, because the tail alone stops being
enough to find at a glance. Two signals, not one: the tail points at the
speaker AND the speaker is the figure in focus.
`face_in` decides which way a figure is drawn. Every character is drawn facing
one way in their sheet and the page mirrors them, so a figure on the right half
of the stage is flipped to face the middle. Nobody ever addresses the edge of

_moves_comment: Somebody walking on or off the stage, and where they walk from or to.
THE STAGE HAS NO DEPTH. An earlier version sized figures near/mid/far to
say how far into the scene they stood, and it was removed: a half-body
figure cropped at the waist stands ON the bottom edge of the frame, so
the only honest axis left is across. Blocking here is left, right, and
on or off — a character cannot be further away, only elsewhere.
`speed` is the author's, per move, because an arrival is sometimes the
event of the panel and sometimes furniture. `snap` is there for the
second kind and costs the reader nothing.

left.is: Off the left-hand edge of the frame

right.is: Off the right-hand edge of the frame

walk.is: The default. Somebody arriving at a normal pace

slow.is: A reluctant entrance, or a long goodbye

snap.is: No movement at all — they are simply there

_bubbles_comment: Four balloon shapes, and the third field of a speaker line chooses one:
**Ti|surprised|shout:** — character, face, shape. `say` is the default and is
These are SHAPES, not volumes, and they are shapes a reader of manga already
knows how to read without being told: the spiked balloon is loud, the cloud is
unspoken, the broken line is quiet. That is why they are worth having — a
shape carries tone without spending a word of the ninety a chapter has, and a
grade-8 reader decodes it for free.
`think` is the one to be careful with. A thought balloon is interior monologue,
and interior monologue is not speech — a listening or speaking exercise cannot
be built on it, and a line that the learner is meant to practise saying must
never be a thought. Use it for what Ti does not say out loud.
There is deliberately no shape for a whisper-that-nobody-hears and no shape for
an off-panel voice. Both need a fifth and sixth contour to learn, and neither
earns its keep in twelve chapters.

bubbles.say: An ordinary line, spoken aloud. Rounded, hard contour, solid tail.
bubbles.shout: Loud — called across a yard, or lost patience. Spiked contour.
bubbles.think: Not said. A cloud, with bubbles trailing to the thinker.
bubbles.whisper: Said quietly, or not meant to carry. Broken contour, no fill weight.

_props_comment: Things that are in the scene. `@item bucket at=left` puts one on the floor of
the panel; `@item board-game at=Ti` puts it beside Ti; `@item none` clears the
stage. A prop PERSISTS across panels until it is cleared or the background
changes, because a bucket does not leave the yard when somebody answers.
Every prop here is one the twelve chapters actually put on stage — this list
was written from research/story/chapter-briefs.md, chapter by chapter, and not
from a guess at what a story might want. A prop nobody names is a drawing
nobody makes, and an unused slug is worse than a missing one: it reads as
available and it is not drawn.
`size` is the prop's height as a fraction of the panel and exists so the page
never has to guess scale from the image. A bucket and a board game are both
about a knee high; a class list pinned to a wall is not on the floor at all,
which is what `hangs` is for.
Drawn as ONE cut-out each, on white, and keyed to transparency by
tools/make_overlay.py — the same border-flood as the character sheets, for the
same reason. Saved as art/props/<slug>.png, published as .webp.
FOUR PROPS WERE RETIRED FROM THIS LIST, and the reason is worth keeping. They
were bucket, lantern, rubbish-bag and chalk, and every one of them was placed
in a scene to use up the vocabulary rather than because the scene contained
it — the bucket in a kitchen that unit 1 says it sits behind, a festival
lantern after chapter 5 released the lanterns onto the water, a sack of beach
litter days before the clean-up, chalk with nobody marking anything. The test
a prop has to pass is whether the dialogue gives the reader a reason to
believe the object is in that place at that moment. Four did not, and four
drawings nobody needed came off the art bill with them.
Their prompts are still in illustration-prompts.md, marked as not currently
placed. If the Skills 1 passages are ever staged the bucket comes straight
back — that is where the fish actually is.

board-game.is: A hand-cut wooden board game, bottle-top counters, a lid that does not fit

class-list.is: A typed class list on a noticeboard, names down the sheet, a curled corner

notebook.is: A school exercise book, open, a pencil across it

green-notebook.is: The keeper's notebook — green cloth cover, salt-stained, swollen with writing

cakes.is: A tray of bánh ít lá gai, dark green leaf parcels, stacked

money.is: A folded fan of banknotes, soft with handling, the top one old

radio.is: A battered transistor radio, aerial up, dial worn bare

phone.is: A cheap phone held up flat, screen showing no signal

box.is: A small metal box, salt-welded shut, no hinge you can see

worksheet.is: A printed school worksheet, questions numbered down it, one left blank

_fx_comment: Manga sign language: transparent overlays that sit ON TOP of a figure or over
the whole frame. `@fx dizzy on=Ti` marks Ti; `@fx rain on=panel` marks the
scene. An effect lasts ONE PANEL and then goes, which is the opposite of a
prop, and it is the right default — an effect is punctuation and punctuation
does not persist. Repeat the line on the next panel if it should.
`over` is where an effect is allowed to go, and the build enforces it. Rain
over one boy is nonsense and a sweat drop over a whole street is nonsense the
other way; getting told at build time beats finding out by looking.
Restraint is the whole discipline here. A panel with a shock burst AND circling
birds AND motion lines is not three times as expressive, it is unreadable — so
the build caps a figure at ONE effect and the panel at ONE, and a chapter that
wants more should want fewer. Two of these (`flush`, `sweat`) do a job the six
drawn faces cannot: embarrassment is not one of the six and would have cost
Drawn as flat cut-outs on white and keyed the same way as the props, except
`rain` and `gloom`, which are drawn as loose full-frame washes.

impact.is: A hard white starburst behind the figure — shock, or a blow landing

sparkle.is: Soft rising glints — the sea working, or something arriving

dizzy.is: Small stars and birds circling above the head, stunned

sweat.is: One large drop at the temple — caught out, or working hard at a lie

flush.is: Pink strokes across the cheeks and ears — embarrassed

anger.is: The cross-shaped popping vein at the temple — lost patience

question.is: One floating question mark — did not follow that

gloom.is: Vertical shadow bars down the figure from above — dread

speed.is: Straight motion lines behind the figure — moving, or moving off

birds.is: Three or four small seabirds crossing the frame

splash.is: A white water burst up the near edge of the frame

rain.is: Slanting rain across the whole frame, grey, no colour
